operation_tail.detail: The CN2025 annex separates provider submissions from information already held by Ofcom; both retain explicit provenance.
The premise base uses AddressBase property information combining Royal Mail postal addresses with additional local-authority property details.
Sub-properties within a building are considered regardless of the number of postal delivery points, preventing one-delivery-point aggregation.
CN2025 used AddressBase Premium and Islands Epoch 119; this historical methodology vintage is not substituted for Spring 2026 Epoch 123.
AddressBase combines NLPG, OS MasterMap address-layer and Royal Mail PAF inputs; the components are recorded as one premise-base lineage.
Each AddressBase BLPU carries a UPRN, spatial reference and one or more land-and-property identifiers; UPRN remains the property identity key.
CN2025 combined AddressBase with the May 2025 2021-Census NSPL and Locale rurality; these auxiliary vintages are kept explicit.
A service-delivery address must be able to receive mail directly or indirectly through a parent, sibling or holding address.
A parent-shell building or site is excluded as a service premise when services are supplied to its individual sub-units.
Included records have no parent address or have a parent classified as a parent-shell, preserving individual service units.
The documented premise construction uses the AddressBase BLPU and classification tables plus the NSPL postcode table.
The methodology joins BLPU postcode_locator to NSPL after uppercasing and removing spaces; normalization does not alter postcode identity.
Only documented AddressBase postal states D, C or L are admitted as addressable objects in the premise-base SQL.
Commercial, residential, dual-use, selected object-of-interest and additional-mail classifications are included only through documented codes.
Premises require approved logical status and an in-use BLPU state of null or 2; other lifecycle states fail closed.
The documented SQL limits countries to England, NI, Scotland and Wales and excludes country J, Channel Islands and Isle of Man.
Fixed provider records are classified as direct UPRN, confident full-address, or approximate street-and-postcode matches rather than one undifferentiated match.
CN2025 received more than 124 million premise-level fixed-availability records; this is methodology context, not a Spring 2026 candidate count.
CN2025 reports 99.7% of its unique premise base matched to at least one provider by UPRN or building-address reference.
The July 2025 match analysis reports 31.4 million premises, 97.1%, matched using UPRN; figures remain bound to that vintage.
A confident non-UPRN address match requires an identified building number or name, street address and postcode.
Approximate matching uses street address and postcode and is not promoted to direct property identity.
Nearly 10,000 initially unmatched CN2025 premises were linked via UPRN parent-child relations, leaving just over 81,000 without a confident match.
Provider records matched only to postcode or to no geography were excluded from CN2025 fixed-coverage analysis.
Ofcom did not use postcode-based estimates to fill unmatched premise coverage, preserving address-level reporting accuracy.
Full-fibre availability requires fibre close enough that only a dedicated connection from the premise to the exchange or access node is needed.
A covered premise may require only a published pre-agreed connection charge; bespoke unknown build costs do not satisfy the definition.
The July 2025 premise base contained 32.4 million premises, including 30.3 million residential; these values are not reused as January 2026 totals.
Availability reporting uses the maximum predicted download speed from any provider covering the premise, not an observed or average speed.
The decent-broadband metric uses at least 10 Mbit/s down and 1 Mbit/s up and explicitly includes premises unmatched to provider records.
Connected Nations fixed coverage covers broadband products and excludes dedicated leased lines that some businesses may use.
CN2025 collected July 2025 active-line data from 57 fixed-network providers and ISPs; this performance source is distinct from availability coverage.
Active-line submissions include retail services and services supplied wholesale to other ISPs, so connection counts are not retail-only.
Full-fibre take-up is estimated against coverage from the same snapshot date to avoid mixing mismatched availability and active-line vintages.
Line speeds may be measured or, where measurements are unavailable, configured for the service; the provenance of the value remains explicit.
From 2024 onward active-speed analysis uses per-line maximum speeds; earlier average-speed series are not treated as directly comparable.
Only active lines assignable to a postcode and reporting speed above zero enter the CN2025 speed analysis.
CN2025 used 18 million qualifying records from about 26.5 million reported lines and weighted them to the reported active-line total.
FWA may use an MNO mobile network shared with mobile users or a WISP dedicated network; the two delivery models remain distinguished.
FWA submissions cover properties serviceable without installing new access points and separately identify whether decent broadband is available.
Ofcom states that the checker property base is updated twice a year, so newly added properties may be absent between updates.
Checker FWA coverage is modelled by operators and localised issues can prevent service at a premise even where coverage is predicted.
Absence of a checker prediction does not prove broadband unavailability; provider websites may contain availability not represented in the checker.
Predicted availability may fail operationally because of property-access permission, maintenance or equipment upgrades; checker output is not an orderability guarantee.
Forty-five official premise-base, matching, speed-method and checker-limit controls were published line by line; candidate counts remain unchanged pending strict r2 bytes.
